## Why this matters {#sec-srt-why}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A sort is the cheapest powerful structure in the book: for $O(n\log n)$ — often a single library call — the array stops being arbitrary. After sorting, the closest pair is a *neighbour*, "how many are smaller" is a *position*, equal values gather into *runs* you can count in one pass, and the best gathering point for absolute errors is the *middle*. Nine times out of ten "just sort it first" is not a hack; it is the whole algorithm, and the scan afterwards is $O(n)$.
:::

The arrays volume has built its tools one at a time: the scan carries state over positions (@sec-arr), prefix sums tabulate positions (@sec-pref), hashing indexes values (@sec-hash), two pointers exploit order (@sec-tp), and sliding windows keep a moving range valid (@sec-sw). The two-pointer chapter could move its two fingers because many of its arrays arrived sorted. **Sorting is how you buy that order when the input never promised it.** This chapter pays the $n\log n$ price and then spends the three things the purchase returns:

- **Neighbours.** Any question about the *closest* or *largest gap between* two values becomes an adjacent scan of $n-1$ pairs instead of $\binom{n}{2}$ (P1).
- **Monotonicity.** Once sorted, predicates that only get harder to the right become searchable: a **binary search** — repeatedly halving a sorted array to find where a value or a threshold sits, $O(\log n)$ probes — and the two-pointer sweeps of @sec-tp are re-licensed at will. (The next chapter, @sec-bst, drills this; here a sorted array is simply a place where "the first index with property $P$" exists and is findable.)
- **Canonical form.** Equal values sit together, so frequencies become runs, ranks become indices, and "the same multiset" becomes "the same string" — the counting and compression patterns (P3, P4) are this sentence with arithmetic.

P5 cashes the deepest fact: sorting puts the **median** in the middle, and the median is the answer to an optimisation question — the exchange argument of @sec-srt-a5. The Sorting Algorithms and Linear-Time Sorting chapters later in this part open the sort box itself (merge sort, quicksort, heapsort, radix sort, the $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound); this chapter stays on the application side of that door, and *uses* sorting as freely as the previous chapters used their tools. The library calls themselves (`sorted`, `key=`, `cmp_to_key`, `std::sort` with a lambda) were introduced in @sec-lang-p3; here we use them.

One note before the lessons. Two classic problems of this topic, Largest Number and Sort Array by Increasing Frequency, are already solved end to end in @sec-lang-p3, where keys and comparators first appeared. This chapter does not re-solve them: P2 and P4 point to those solutions with a short card, and solve a Codeforces problem in their place that adds a new idea (an exchange-argument comparator in @sec-srt-p2-b, a sort over counts in @sec-srt-p4-b). Part A is five lessons; Part B is five patterns with ten solved problems.

## A1. What a sort buys: stability, neighbours, monotonicity {#sec-srt-a1}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Two guarantees, one price. **(1) Order:** the output is non-decreasing, so equal values form contiguous runs and the array becomes a place where you can search, sweep, and count. **(2) Stability** (Python's `sorted`, C++'s `stable_sort`): elements that compare equal keep their *input* order, so you can sort by one field, then by another, and the second sort preserves the first's work inside ties. The price is $O(n\log n)$ comparisons for a general comparison sort — and the free lunch is that everything *after* the sort is usually linear.
:::

Read the guarantee as a shopping list of structures. After `b = sorted(a)`: the **closest pair** is some $b[i+1] - b[i]$ (P1's lemma); **equal values are contiguous**, so a histogram is one linear pass over runs (P3); the array is **monotone**, so thresholds answer to binary search and two fingers never rewind (the licence of @sec-tp, now purchasable); and sorting by a **derived value** costs one extra key function, not a new algorithm (P4). Stability is the quiet one: it is exactly what lets you "sort by grade, ties by name" by sorting twice, the tie-break field first. Python's `sorted` and `list.sort` are guaranteed stable by the language documentation; C++ `std::sort` is not (it is usually an introsort), and `std::stable_sort` is the stable alternative.

```text
b = sort(a, by key)              # O(n log n) once; buys, for every later question:
  neighbours   closest/smallest gap is some b[i+1] - b[i]
  runs         equal keys occupy contiguous blocks -> count in one pass
  monotone     "first index with P" findable by binary search, sweepable by two pointers
  stability    ties keep previous order -> sort twice to sort by two fields
```

The invariant of anything that happens after a sort is worth stating once: **`b` is non-decreasing and a permutation of `a`** — every later scan may assume neighbours are comparable, and may never assume anything about *which* of the equal elements came first unless stability promised it.

Sorting by the **secondary** key (name) first and the **primary** key (grade) last is the stable-composition recipe: the final, most-significant sort is stable, so it groups by grade while leaving the alphabetical order it inherited intact inside each grade block. Do it in the other order — grade first, then name — and the last (name) pass is primary and the grade blocks vanish; make the last pass an unstable `std::sort` and the surviving order inside a tie is arbitrary.

:::

``` {.python .cell-code}
recs = [("Bob", "A"), ("Ann", "B"), ("Cid", "A"), ("Eve", "A"), ("Dan", "B")]

s2 = sorted(s1, key=lambda r: r[1])                 # primary key (grade) last, stable
assert s2 == [("Bob", "A"), ("Cid", "A"), ("Eve", "A"), ("Ann", "B"), ("Dan", "B")]

assert sorted(recs, key=lambda r: (r[1], r[0])) == s2

# reorder the names inside a grade block
b = sorted([4, 2, 1, 3])
assert b == [1, 2, 3, 4]
assert all(b[i + 1] - b[i] >= 0 for i in range(len(b) - 1))   # runs, gaps, monotone
print("a1 demo OK")
```

The demo is small on purpose; the *price discipline* is the lesson. If a question is answered by one scan over an unsorted array (a sum, a max, a membership count), do not sort. If the answer talks about **pairs of values** — closest, gap, overlap, "for each $x$ the smallest $y \ge x$" — the $O(n\log n)$ sort repays itself immediately, because the $O(n)$ scan afterwards replaces an $O(n^2)$ search. That trade is the sentence behind every problem in Part B.

## A2. Comparators: strict weak ordering, several keys, sorting indices {#sec-srt-a2}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A sort needs only one fact about your data: a rule `less(x, y)` answering "must $x$ come before $y$?". Three rules make that rule *usable*: nothing is less than itself (**irreflexive**); the relation is transitive; and "incomparable" (neither less) is transitive too — which forces **ties to form contiguous blocks**. That package is a **strict weak ordering**; `std::sort` demands it and behaves undefined-but-catastrophically without it. Python dodges the whole contract by taking a **key** — one number per element — and ties inherit input order (stability). Two habits unlock everything: sort by a **tuple** for several criteria (negate or invert the descending ones), and **sort indices instead of values** when the values live in parallel arrays or must not move.
:::

@sec-lang-p3 introduced both forms and the C++ rule behind them (@sec-lang-cpp); this lesson adds what problems demand on top: how to *check* a comparator, how to sort several keys with mixed directions, and how to sort positions instead of values. Python's `sorted(a, key=...)` and C++'s `sort(v.begin(), v.end(), comp)` are two different pacts. The key form computes $f(x)$ once per element and compares *numbers*; "who goes first" never depends on the partner, so any key is legal and ties are stable by contract. The comparator form asks *pairs*; it can express orders no key can (Largest Number's $a{+}b$ against $b{+}a$, @sec-lang-p3-largest) — but only if `comp` is a strict weak ordering. The canonical violation is writing `return a.grade <= b.grade;`: with `<=`, an element is "less than" an equal partner, `std::sort`'s partition logic can walk off the end of the array, and you get a wrong answer or a crash. `cmp_to_key` is the bridge: wrap a three-way comparator (`-1/0/1`) and Python supplies the rest.

```text
key form    sorted(a, key=lambda x: (k1, -k2))    # k1 ascending, k2 descending; ties: input order
cmp form    sort(a, comp)  where comp(x, y) = "x strictly before y?"
            must be a strict weak ordering: never return comp as x <= y
index form  order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: a[i])   # values stay put;
            order is a permutation; touch a[i] through it
```

``` {.python .cell-code}
def cmp3(a, b):                       # longer string first; equal length, larger value first
    if len(a) != len(b):
        return -1 if len(a) > len(b) else 1
    ia, ib = int(a), int(b)
    return -1 if ia > ib else (1 if ia < ib else 0)      # a three-way answer
assert [int(d) for d in sorted(["123", "45", "678", "9"], key=cmp_to_key(cmp3))] == \
    [678, 123, 45, 9]                 # 678 before 123: same length, larger value leads

scores = [85, 90, 85, 78]
order = sorted(range(4), key=lambda i: -scores[i])     # sort the indices, not the values
assert order == [1, 0, 2, 3]
assert [scores[i] for i in order] == [90, 85, 85, 78]
# the same order as a tuple key: negate the descending criterion
assert sorted(range(4), key=lambda i: (-scores[i], i)) == order
print("a2 demo OK")
```

A comparator can be tested like any other function. The three conditions are statements about all pairs and triples, so on a small random sample you can check them directly; a `<=` comparator fails the first test immediately.

::: {#arr-srt-a2-swo .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def is_strict_weak(items, less):
    """Check the three conditions of a strict weak ordering on a small sample."""
    for x in items:
        if less(x, x):                                 # irreflexive
            return False
    for x in items:
        for y in items:
            for z in items:
                if less(x, y) and less(y, z) and not less(x, z):
                    return False                       # transitive
                inc = lambda u, v: not less(u, v) and not less(v, u)
                if inc(x, y) and inc(y, z) and not inc(x, z):
                    return False                       # ties are transitive
    return True

sample = [random.randint(0, 5) for _ in range(8)]
assert is_strict_weak(sample, lambda x, y: x < y)
assert not is_strict_weak(sample, lambda x, y: x <= y)          # the classic bug
# a rule that is not even transitive: "x before y if they differ by exactly 1"
assert not is_strict_weak([1, 2, 3], lambda x, y: y - x == 1)
# the pairwise concatenation rule of Largest Number passes on random strings
words = [str(random.randint(0, 120)) for _ in range(7)]
assert is_strict_weak(words, lambda a, b: a + b > b + a)
# the exchange rule of Robot Vacuum Cleaner (@sec-srt-p2-b) passes too
sh = [(random.randint(0, 3), random.randint(0, 3)) for _ in range(7)]
sh = [p for p in sh if p != (0, 0)]
assert is_strict_weak(sh, lambda a, b: a[0] * b[1] > b[0] * a[1])
print("strict weak ordering checks OK")
```


Passing on a sample is evidence, not a proof; the proof is an argument like "this rule compares $f(a)$ with $f(b)$ for some number $f$", which is how @sec-srt-p2-b turns its comparator into a key.

Two design notes the stress of real problems will demand. First, **prefer a key over a comparator** whenever the rule compares each element to *nothing but itself* — keys run once per element, comparators run $O(n\log n)$ times, and a wrong comparator is a correctness bug while a slow key is just slow. Second, a pairwise comparator must be **provable**, not intuitive: Largest Number's $a{+}b > b{+}a$ looks transitive but needs an actual proof (@sec-lang-p3-largest gives it); when in doubt, test your comparator against a brute-force scan of all pair arrangements on random small inputs, exactly the habit every solved problem here stress-tests with.

## A3. Non-comparison sorts: counting, bucket, radix, and their limits {#sec-srt-a3}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Comparison sorts pay in *questions* ("is $x < y$?"), and $\Omega(n\log n)$ questions are necessary in general. Non-comparison sorts pay in **structure of the values** instead. **Counting sort** tallies each value in a `count[v]` array indexed *by value*, then walks $v = 0 \dots V{-}1$ emitting copies: $O(n + V)$, no comparisons ever. **Bucket sort** scatters values into wide buckets and sorts (or reasons about) each: $O(n + B)$ when values spread evenly — or, the contest version, when you can *prove* the answer never hides inside a bucket (@sec-srt-p3-b). **Radix sort** sorts digit by digit with a *stable* counting sort, cheapest-key-first: $O(\text{digits} \cdot (n + \text{base}))$. Each is linear, each has a price tag, and the price tag is the lesson.
:::

The three price tags: counting sort needs the **range** $V$ small — it allocates and walks $V$ cells, so $n = 10^5$ values up to $10^9$ is a $10^9$-cell, $10^9$-step table. Bucket sort needs a **guarantee** — even spread (uniform inputs, sort each bucket) or a structural proof that only bucket *extremes* matter; scatter into arbitrary buckets and sort each the wrong way and you have quicksort with extra steps. Radix needs **fixed-length keys over a small alphabet** (non-negative integers, padded strings); it is linear with a big constant and rarely beats `std::sort` unless $n$ is huge and the keys are short. And the escape hatch when all three prices are too high: **coordinate compression** (@sec-srt-a4) shrinks a $10^9$ *value* range to an $n$ *rank* range — you cannot count $10^9$ values, but you can always count $n$ ranks.

```text
counting   cnt = array(V); for x: cnt[x] += 1; for v in 0..V-1: emit v  cnt[v] times
           O(n + V) - needs small V
bucket     b = bucket_of(x) by position in [min, max]; scatter, sort/scan each
           O(n + B) - needs spread or a theorem about what matters
radix      for each digit, low to high: STABLE counting sort by that digit
           O(d(n + B)) - needs fixed-length, small-alphabet keys
merge sort, quicksort, quickselect: the Sorting Algorithms chapter
```

The linear sorts earn their speed only when their *precondition* is written in the constraints — a fixed small range (the $0 \dots 1000$ of @sec-srt-p3-a), provable irrelevance of within-bucket detail (@sec-srt-p3-b), or short fixed keys.
``` {.python .cell-code}
def counting_sort(a, V):
    cnt = [0] * V
    for x in a:
        cnt[x] += 1
    out = []
    for v in range(V):                    # values in order; cnt[v] copies each
        out += [v] * cnt[v]
    return out

def radix_sort(a):                        # non-negative ints, LSD radix, base 10
    out = list(a)
    width = max((len(str(x)) for x in out), default=1)
    for d in range(width):                # least significant digit first
        buckets = [[] for _ in range(10)]
        for x in out:
            buckets[(x // 10 ** d) % 10].append(x)
        out = [x for b in buckets for x in b]   # concatenation IS the stable sort
    return out

def counting_sort_stable(items, key, V):          # records, not just numbers
    cnt = [0] * (V + 1)
    for it in items:
        cnt[key(it) + 1] += 1
    for v in range(V):                    # prefix sums: cnt[v] = first slot of key v
        cnt[v + 1] += cnt[v]
    out = [None] * len(items)
    for it in items:                      # left to right: equal keys keep input order
        out[cnt[key(it)]] = it
        cnt[key(it)] += 1
    return out

for _ in range(300):
    a = [random.randrange(1000) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 20))]
    assert counting_sort(a, 1000) == sorted(a)
    assert radix_sort(a) == sorted(a)
    recs = [(random.randrange(5), i) for i in range(random.randint(0, 12))]
    assert counting_sort_stable(recs, lambda r: r[0], 5) == sorted(recs, key=lambda r: r[0])
assert counting_sort([2, 0, 2, 1], 3) == [0, 1, 2, 2]
assert radix_sort([170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66]) == [2, 24, 45, 66, 75, 90, 170, 802]
print("a3 demo OK")
```

## A4. Ranks and coordinate compression in one line {#sec-srt-a4}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
When only the **relative order** of values matters — ranks, "smaller than how many?", adjacency in a Fenwick tree or segment tree over *values* — the magnitudes are decoration. **Coordinate compression** replaces every value by its position in the sorted list of distinct values: huge sparse numbers ($-10^9 \dots 10^9$) become dense indices $1 \dots n$. The entire recipe is one line: `rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(a)))}`, then look each element up. It is *not* a sorting algorithm; it is sorting used as a translation device, and it is the reason "values up to $10^9$" in a statement is no longer scary.
:::

Three variants, one idea. **Rank with ties** (equal values share a rank): compress `set(a)` — @sec-srt-p4-a's LC 1331. **Index without ties** (a strict order even for equal values, e.g. "the $i$-th occurrence"): sort `enumerate(a)` pairs — pairs sort tie-safe because the index breaks every tie. **Value range to table index**: when an array is indexed by value and the values are merely *sparse* (a few of $10^9$), compression turns a $10^9$ table into $n+1$ cells — the same move A3's price tag demands, paid in one sort instead of a bigger table.

```text
rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(a)))}   # dict comprehension:
  set(a)      collapse duplicates        -> ties share a rank
  sorted      increasing distinct values -> ranks are dense 1..|set|
  enumerate   position becomes the rank  -> lookup per element is O(1)
```

## A5. Sorting to minimise a cost: the median and exchange arguments {#sec-srt-a5}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Sorting is not only a preprocessing step — it *is* the algorithm for a family of optimisation problems, proved by an **exchange argument** (@sec-pf-greedy): show that any solution violating the sorted order can be swapped into sorted order without getting worse, so a best solution is sorted. The flagship: gather everyone to one point, paying distance — $\min_t \sum_i |x_i - t|$ — and the answer is the **median**, the middle of the sorted list. The proof is a slide: move $t$ one step right and the cost changes by (how many sit to the left) minus (how many sit to the right); the change flips sign exactly once, at the middle. Mean? That minimises *squared* deviations — a different objective; absolute values are the median's territory.
:::

Two faces of the same proof technique. **Ordering exchanges** say the *arrangement* is optimal: Largest Number's swap proof (@sec-lang-p3-largest) shows any adjacent inversion $a{+}b < b{+}a$ can be swapped without decreasing the number, so the best arrangement is comparator-sorted. **Position exchanges** say the *location* is optimal: the median slide above, and its weighted version — treat a value with cost $c$ as $c$ clones of a unit-price stick at that spot, run the same slide with counts replaced by weights, and the flip point becomes the **weighted median**: the first position whose cumulative weight reaches half the total (@sec-srt-p5-b). Both faces need no algorithm theory — just "if it were out of order, swapping would help", checked once, then sortedness does the rest.

```text
minimise  sum |x_i - t|          -> any median of the x_i   (slide: cost changes by
                                     #left - #right; flips sign only at the middle)
minimise  sum w_i |x_i - t|      -> weighted median: sort pairs by x, walk cumulative
                                     w, stop at 2*cum >= total
maximise  concatenation          -> exchange adjacent pairs: sort by the pairwise rule
                                     (a+b beats b+a) - proof per ordering, not per element
```

## Pattern 1: Sort, then scan neighbours {#sec-srt-p1}

**Where we are.** Part A listed what a sort buys; Part B spends it in five steps, each adding one idea to the last. P1 spends the plainest purchase, *neighbours*: sort by value, and the answer sits between adjacent elements. P2 changes **which order** you sort into: a rule you design from the problem and prove consistent. P3 changes **how** you sort: when the values are small, or only their position in a range matters, skip comparisons altogether. P4 changes **what you sort on**: ranks, or counts computed from the whole array. P5 uses the sorted order to **place a point**: the median and its weighted version.

Pattern 1 is A1's first purchase: sortedness makes the answer **local**. Over an unsorted array, "the two closest values" or "the biggest successive gap" hides among $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs; over a sorted array it is always realised by two *neighbours*, so one $O(n)$ pass over $n-1$ adjacent pairs finishes the job. Both problems here are the very same scan — one wants the smallest gap (Minimum Absolute Difference), the other wants the smallest gap dressed as a team split (Honest Coach).

**Recognise it.** "Minimum absolute difference between any two elements", "closest pair", "split into two groups minimising the gap at the seam", or any extremum over *pairs of values* where the values themselves carry no positional meaning. Constraints $n \le 10^5$ rule out the $O(n^2)$ pair loop and price in one $O(n\log n)$ sort.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Sort once; the answer is between neighbours.

```text
b = sorted(a)
best = min(b[i+1] - b[i] for i in 0 .. n-2)     # smallest gap
# collect every pair that ties it, or take the seam directly
```

**Invariant.** For $i < j$, $b[j] - b[i]$ is a *sum* of adjacent gaps, so it is never smaller than the least adjacent gap; hence $\min$ over all pairs $= \min$ over the $n-1$ adjacent pairs, and every optimal pair is adjacent in sorted order.
:::

**Complexity.** $O(n\log n)$ time (the sort dominates; the scan is $O(n)$), $O(n)$ space for the sorted copy. The brute $O(n^2)$ pair scan is the oracle both problems test against.

### Problem: Minimum Absolute Difference {#sec-srt-p1-a}

::: {.p-statement}
An array `arr` of $n$ **distinct** integers ($2 \le n \le 10^5$, $-10^6 \le \mathit{arr}[i] \le 10^6$). Find every pair of elements whose absolute difference equals the smallest absolute difference attained by *any* pair, and return those pairs as $[a, b]$ with $a < b$, listed in ascending order.

Source: [LC 1200 · Minimum Absolute Difference](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-absolute-difference/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Over all $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs the closest two numbers are easy to miss, but sorting changes the picture: **once the array is sorted, the minimum difference is attained by some *adjacent* pair.** If $x < y < z$, then $z - x = (y - x) + (z - y)$ is at least each of the two smaller gaps, so a pair with a value between them is never strictly closer than a neighbouring pair. That collapses $O(n^2)$ pair checks into one $O(n)$ scan of $n-1$ gaps, down a sorted array. This is @sec-srt-p1's thesis: sort, then look only at neighbours.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every pair.** For each $i < j$ compute $|\mathit{arr}[i] - \mathit{arr}[j]|$, keep the smallest, and collect every pair at that distance. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space — the oracle that proves the fast form.
2. **Insertion sort, then scan neighbours.** Get sortedness the honest way — sink each element into the sorted prefix with adjacent swaps — then run the neighbour scan. Same $O(n^2)$ *time* as the brute force in the worst case (best case $O(n)$ on nearly-sorted input), but the two halves of the work are cleanly separated: sorting is the reusable tool, the scan is the pattern.
3. **Sort with the built-in, then scan neighbours.** Sort once via `sorted()` / `std::sort`; the answer gaps are all $\le$ any non-adjacent gap, so a single left-to-right pass over adjacent differences finds the minimum *and* collects the pairs realising it. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space for the sorted copy.

**Invariant.** After sorting into `b`, every pair's difference is at least the smallest adjacent gap, so $\text{best} = \min_i (b[i+1] - b[i])$; the required answer is exactly the adjacent pairs whose gap equals `best` (already produced in ascending order).
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

#### Insertion sort, then scan neighbours

::: {.form-next}
Take the *sorting half* of the fast form seriously: get the array into ascending order with the hand-written $O(n^2)$ insertion sort, then reuse the neighbour scan verbatim. Same worst-case $O(n^2)$ time as the brute force (but $O(n)$ on a nearly-sorted input), and the *point* is the split — the pair scan is replaced by "sort, then $n-1$ neighbour checks", and only the sortedness step still costs quadratic time. The next rung hands that step to the language's built-in sort and the whole thing collapses to $O(n\log n)$.

**Insertion sort, in plain words** (the Sorting Algorithms chapter studies it properly). Walk the array left to right. At each index, sink the new element toward the front by swapping it with its left neighbour while that neighbour is bigger. After $i$ passes, the first $i{+}1$ positions are sorted, and nothing to their right has been touched. Cost is $O(n^2)$ worst case (a reverse-sorted input), $O(n)$ best case (already sorted), $O(1)$ extra space.

**Worked example.** arr $= [4, 2, 1, 3]$. Pass 1 sinks $2$ past $4$: $[2, 4, 1, 3]$. Pass 2 sinks $1$ twice: $[1, 2, 4, 3]$. Pass 3 sinks $3$ past $4$: $[1, 2, 3, 4]$. Then one neighbour scan sees gaps $1, 1, 1$ — minimum $1$, three winning pairs.

Once sorted, the scan is $O(n)$ and — this is the reusable prize — every "closest pair", "smallest gap", "minimum difference" question becomes an adjacent scan, which is why @sec-srt-p1-b is the *same* code with a story change.

### Problem: Honest Coach {#sec-srt-p1-b}

::: {.p-statement}

Each test case gives $n$ athletes ($2 \le n \le 50$) with strengths $s_1, \dots, s_n$ ($1 \le s_i \le 1000$). Split them into **two non-empty teams** $A$ and $B$ so that the value $|\max(A) - \min(B)|$ is as small as possible — the coach wants the strongest athlete of one team to be as close as possible to the weakest of the other. Print that minimum value. The first input line is $t$ ($1 \le t \le 1000$), the number of test cases.

Source: [CF 1360B · Honest Coach](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1360/B){.solved rating="800"}

Example — one test case: $n = 5$, $s = [3, 1, 2, 6, 4]$. Output $1$ (put $[1,2,3]$ in one team and $[4,6]$ in the other: the seam is $|3 - 4| = 1$).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The seam $|\max(A) - \min(B)|$ is realised by **two athletes sitting next to each other in the sorted order.** Sort the strengths. Two facts finish it. Any split gives $|\max(A) - \min(B)|$ equal to the difference of two different athletes, so it is at least the smallest difference between any two athletes, which is the smallest adjacent gap $g$ of the sorted array. And cutting the sorted array at that gap (left part to $A$, right part to $B$) achieves exactly $g$. So the answer is the smallest adjacent gap. This is the very same "sort, then scan neighbours" move as @sec-srt-p1-a, wearing a story about teams instead of pairs.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every pair.** For each $i < j$ record $|s_i - s_j|$ and keep the minimum. That minimum is a lower bound on every split's seam (a seam is always the difference of two athletes), and the closest pair is achievable (see the invariant). $O(n^2)$ time — the oracle.
2. **Insertion sort, then take the smallest adjacent gap.** Buy sortedness with the hand-written $O(n^2)$ insertion sort, then run the same $n-1$ neighbour scan. Same asymptotic time as the pair scan in the worst case, but the two ideas (sorting, adjacent gap) are separated so you can see which half the pattern actually uses.
3. **Sort, then take the smallest adjacent gap.** Sort with the built-in; answer $= \min_i (s[i+1] - s[i])$. $O(n\log n)$ time.

**Invariant.** Lower bound: for any split, $|\max(A) - \min(B)|$ is $|s_i - s_j|$ for two different athletes, so it is $\ge$ the smallest pair difference, which equals the smallest adjacent gap of the sorted array (@sec-srt-p1-a). Achievability: if that gap sits between $b_k$ and $b_{k+1}$, put $b_0 \dots b_k$ in $A$ and the rest in $B$; then $\max(A) = b_k$ and $\min(B) = b_{k+1}$. So answer $= \min$ adjacent gap.
:::

## Pattern 2: Custom comparators {#sec-srt-p2}

**From the value order to an order you design.** Pattern 1 sorted by the values themselves; the only design choice was to sort at all. Sometimes the correct order is not "by value" but "by a rule the problem forces on you", and the whole algorithm is a single sort once that rule is stated as a valid comparator (A2's contract). Queue Reconstruction needs a *two-key* order with mixed directions (height down, $k$ up) and a greedy insertion after it; Robot Vacuum Cleaner needs a genuinely *pairwise* rule, derived from an exchange argument and then shown to be a key in disguise.

**Recognise it.** "Largest number by concatenating", "rearrange so that $a$ before $b$ iff some pairwise test holds", "rebuild an order from partial constraints", or any greedy that first sorts by a rule involving *two* elements together. The tell is that the ordering depends on a **pair**, not on each element's own score — so you need a comparator (`cmp_to_key`, a C++ lambda), not just a key.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Turn the rule into an order; prove it is a strict weak ordering; sort.

```text
key form   sorted(a, key=lambda x: (k1, -k2))        # several criteria, mixed directions
cmp  form  cmp_to_key(comp)  /  sort(v, comp)        # pairwise rule:
           comp(a, b) = "a strictly before b?"  - never <=  (strict weak ordering)
tie-safe   include the index in the key: sort indices when values must not move
```

**Invariant.** The comparator agrees with a genuine total order on the (possibly tied) items — irreflexive, transitive, ties transitive — so the sort produces one canonical arrangement and `std::sort`'s partitioning never walks off an endpoint.
:::

**Complexity.** $O(n\log n)$ comparisons (each costing whatever the rule costs — for string concatenation, the string length); Python caches a key per element, so a *key* sort is $O(n\log n)$ comparisons on $n$ precomputed scores. The design work is proving the comparator, not the sort.

### Problem: Queue Reconstruction by Height {#sec-srt-p2-a}

::: {.p-statement}
An array `people` of $n$ people ($1 \le n \le 2000$), each written $[h, k]$: height $h$ ($0 \le h \le 10^6$) and $k$ ($0 \le k < n$) = the number of people who must stand **in front of** them with height $\ge h$. Rebuild the queue: return an ordering in which every person's $k$ is correct. It is guaranteed at least one ordering exists.

Source: [LC 406 · Queue Reconstruction by Height](https://leetcode.com/problems/queue-reconstruction-by-height/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example: input $[[7,0],[4,4],[7,1],[5,0],[6,1],[5,2]]$ → output $[[5,0],[7,0],[5,2],[6,1],[4,4],[7,1]]$.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A person's $k$ only counts people **at least as tall** as them, so short people are invisible to the constraints of tall people. Process from the **tallest down**: when you place a height-$h$ person, everyone already placed is $\ge h$, so their $k$ is exactly "the number of already-placed people in front of me" — and you can drop them into the queue at **index $k$** like inserting into a line. Because later (shorter) insertions land in front of or behind without changing how many *taller-or-equal* people sit ahead of an already-placed person, earlier placements never break. The whole method hangs on one **custom comparator**: sort by height descending, and — crucially — by $k$ ascending among equal heights so that two people of the same height slot into each other correctly. This is @sec-srt-p2's "sorting by several keys," and it pairs with the concatenated-string comparator of Largest Number (@sec-lang-p3-largest).
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every ordering.** Enumerate all $n!$ permutations and keep the first that satisfies every person's $k$-count. $O(n! \cdot n)$ time — a genuine oracle, usable only for tiny $n$.
2. **Short-first, k-th empty slot.** Sort by $(h, -k)$ (shortest first, ties broken by $k$ descending), then walk that order placing each person at the $k$-th *empty* slot of a length-$n$ array. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(n)$ space — a legitimate middle rung that reaches the same answer as form 3 with a mirrored comparator and different bookkeeping (write-into-slot instead of insert-into-list).
3. **Tall-first sort, insert at index $k$.** Sort by $(-h, k)$; walk that order inserting each person at position $k$ of a growing list. $O(n^2)$ time ($n$ inserts, each $O(n)$ shifting), $O(n)$ space — the accepted greedy, powered by a two-key comparator.

**Invariant.** After placing the tallest $m$ distinct height levels, the partially built queue already satisfies every placed person's $k$, and inserting a shorter person at index $k$ changes no placed person's taller-or-equal front-count (the new person is shorter, so is not counted). Form 2's invariant is the mirror: after placing the shortest $m$ levels, every empty slot ahead of the current person is reserved for someone taller than us, so the $k$-th empty slot is exactly the index where $k$ taller-or-equal people will end up in front.
:::

#### Sort short-first, drop into the k-th empty slot

::: {.form-next}
Reverse the direction and change the bookkeeping. Sort by **height ascending, $k$ descending**, allocate a length-$n$ array of empty slots, and drop each person into the slot at index $k$ among the still-empty cells. Same $O(n^2)$ total as form 3 (each person scans the empty-slot list), but with a mirrored comparator and a different data-structure choice: pre-allocated slots with positional writes instead of a growing list with `insert`. The next rung flips the direction back to tall-first and lets a plain list-insert do the work — same complexity, simpler code.

**Why short-first also works, in plain words.** When the current person is height $h$, every person already placed has height $\le h$ — so they will count toward our $k$ **only if we stand behind them**. Every empty slot will later be filled by someone at least as tall as us (everyone not yet placed is taller, or equally tall with a smaller $k$), and every filled slot holds someone who does not count for us (shorter, or equally tall but standing behind us). So taking the $k$-th empty slot (0-based) leaves exactly $k$ empty slots in front, which become exactly $k$ taller-or-equal people. Ties broken by $k$ **descending**, because two equal-height people count each other, and the one wanting more people in front must be placed later.

**Worked example.** people $= [[7,0],[4,4],[7,1],[5,0],[6,1],[5,2]]$. Sort by $(h, -k)$ → $[4,4],[5,2],[5,0],[6,1],[7,1],[7,0]$. Six empty slots $[\_,\_,\_,\_,\_,\_]$. Place $[4,4]$: 6 empties, take the 4th → index 4. Place $[5,2]$: empties $\{0,1,2,3,5\}$, take the 2nd → index 2. Place $[5,0]$: empties $\{0,1,3,5\}$, take the 0th → index 0. Place $[6,1]$: empties $\{1,3,5\}$, take the 1st → index 3. Place $[7,1]$: empties $\{1,5\}$, take the 1st → index 5. Place $[7,0]$: empties $\{1\}$, take the 0th → index 1. Final queue $[[5,0],[7,0],[5,2],[6,1],[4,4],[7,1]]$ — identical to form 3's answer, reached by an opposite-direction walk.

::: {.form-next}
The greedy that sorting unlocks — and the shortest way to write the two-key insight. Order people by **height descending, $k$ ascending**, then insert each into a growing list at position $k$. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(n)$ space. Reversing the tie-break would let the first person see the second ahead and over-count — a wrong queue.

### Problem: Robot Vacuum Cleaner {#sec-srt-p2-b}

::: {.p-statement}
You are given $n$ non-empty strings $t_1, \dots, t_n$ made only of the letters `s` and `h` ($1 \le n \le 10^5$, total length at most $10^5$). Concatenate all of them, each exactly once, in an order you choose. The **noise** of the result is the number of pairs of positions $i < j$ with an `s` at $i$ and an `h` at $j$ (the number of `sh` subsequences). Print the maximum possible noise.

Source: [CF 922D · Robot Vacuum Cleaner](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/922/D){.solved rating="1800"}

Example: strings `ssh`, `hs`, `s`, `hhhs` → $18$ (the order `s`, `ssh`, `hs`, `hhhs` gives `ssshhshhhs`). Strings `h`, `s` → $1$ (order `s`, `h`).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Swapping two neighbouring strings $a, b$ changes only the `sh` pairs that cross between them: with $a$ first there are $s(a)\cdot h(b)$ of them, with $b$ first $s(b)\cdot h(a)$, where $s(x)$ and $h(x)$ count the letters of $x$. Every other pair keeps its order. So put $a$ before $b$ when $s(a)\,h(b) > s(b)\,h(a)$, sort with that pairwise rule, and count. The rule is the same as ordering by the ratio $s/h$ from large to small, which proves it is a valid strict weak ordering.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every order.** Enumerate all $n!$ orders, build each concatenation, count its `sh` pairs, keep the largest. Exponential: a test oracle for $n \le 6$.
2. **Sort with the exchange comparator.** Count $s(x)$ and $h(x)$ for every string. Sort with "$a$ before $b$ iff $s(a)h(b) > s(b)h(a)$" (cross-multiplied, so no division), concatenate, and count the pairs in one left-to-right pass: keep the number of `s` seen so far and add it at every `h`. $O(n\log n + L)$ where $L$ is the total length.
3. **A key instead of a comparator, and no concatenation.** The comparator compares the fractions $s/h$, so a key (the fraction, with $h = 0$ meaning "infinitely large") gives the same order. While walking the sorted strings, add `seen_s * h(x)` for the pairs that cross into $x$ plus the pairs inside $x$, without ever building the long string.

**Invariant.** Exchange argument (@sec-pf-greedy): if two adjacent strings break the rule, swapping them raises the noise by $s(b)h(a) - s(a)h(b) > 0$, so an optimal order has no adjacent violation; and swapping two *tied* neighbours leaves the noise unchanged, so every order sorted by the rule has the same, maximal, noise.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

## Pattern 3: Counting and bucket sort {#sec-srt-p3}

**From designing the order to skipping comparisons.** Patterns 1 and 2 always paid $O(n\log n)$ comparisons; only the order changed. Pattern 3 keeps the order fixed and changes *how* it is produced, using A3's linear sorts on real inputs. When the **value range** is small, counting sort beats every comparison sort by indexing `count[v]` directly; when the range is huge but the answer provably lives *between* buckets, bucket sort plus the pigeonhole principle keeps it linear anyway. Relative Sort Array is the counting case ($0 \le v \le 1000$); Maximum Gap is the bucket case ($v$ up to $10^9$, histogram impossible).

**Recognise it.** Values bounded by a small constant ($\le 10^3$–$10^6$) with an order to respect → counting sort. Or a "maximum successive difference after sorting" over a huge range where $O(n\log n)$ is explicitly disallowed → bucket + pigeonhole. Or a fixed tiny alphabet (colours, 3 values) → counting in place.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Index by value (counting), or by position-in-range (bucket).

```text
counting   cnt = [0]*V; for x: cnt[x] += 1; for v in 0..V-1: emit v cnt[v] times
           O(n + V) - only when V is small; arr2-first then leftovers = a custom emit order
bucket     width = max(1, (mx-mn)//(n-1)); b = (x-mn)//width; keep only per-bucket min,max
           answer = max over seams: min of a non-empty bucket - max of the previous one
```

**Invariant.** Counting: emitting value $v$ exactly `cnt[v]` times preserves the multiset, and the *walk order* is the sort order. Bucket: the $n-1$ gaps add up to $\max - \min$, so the largest is at least their average, which is $\ge$ the bucket width (pigeonhole); a within-bucket difference is at most width $-1$, so the max gap always joins two different buckets, and storing only per-bucket extremes loses nothing.
:::

**Complexity.** Counting $O(n + V)$ time, $O(V)$ space — linear when $V$ is a small constant. Bucket $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space. Both strictly beat the $O(n\log n)$ comparison route *because* they exploit value structure the comparison model is blind to.

### Problem: Relative Sort Array {#sec-srt-p3-a}

::: {.p-statement}
Two arrays `arr1` and `arr2` ($1 \le$ lengths $\le 1000$, $0 \le$ values $\le 1000$). `arr2`'s elements are **distinct** and all appear in `arr1`. Reorder `arr1` so that equal elements are grouped and the first appearance of each value follows `arr2`'s order; values not in `arr2` go at the **end in ascending order**.

Source: [LC 1122 · Relative Sort Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/relative-sort-array/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}

Example: `arr1 = [2,3,1,3,2,4,6,7,9,2,19]`, `arr2 = [2,1,4,3,9,6]` → `[2,2,2,1,4,3,3,9,6,7,19]`.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
`arr2` is a *hand-written sort order* for the values it names; everything else sorts normally and trails. Two natural tools fit. A **custom key** maps each value to its index in `arr2` (with a big sentinel for absent values) and lets a comparison sort obey the map — the @sec-srt-p2 comparator idea again. But the values are tiny ($0 \le v \le 1000$), so a **counting sort** is better: build a histogram, then *emit* each value the number of times it occurs, walking `arr2` first and the leftover values in ascending order. No comparisons at all — the value range is small enough to index directly, which is A3's promise.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Selection sort with the $(\text{rank}, \text{value})$ key.** Repeatedly pull the smallest remaining element under the two-part key and append it to the answer. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(n)$ extra for the rank map and the working copy — the *definition* of "sort by key", without borrowing a sort.
2. **Key sort via an order map.** Give each value a key $(\text{its index in } arr2 \text{ or } \infty,\ \text{value})$ and sort `arr1` by that key: $O(n\log n)$ time. The `arr2`-values get distinct small keys (so they group and follow `arr2`); the rest share the $\infty$ primary key and so sort by their value ascending.
3. **Counting sort (histogram + emit).** `count[v]` for each value $0..1000$; append each `arr2` value `count` times, then every remaining value in ascending order `count` times. $O(n + V)$ time, $O(V)$ space.

**Invariant.** Emitting a value exactly `count[value]` times preserves its multiplicity, and visiting `arr2` before the ascending leftover sweep makes the output order equal "`arr2` order, then ascending" for all values.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

#### Selection sort on the (rank, value) key

::: {.form-next}
Before we let a language sort for us, let's *be* the sort. Selection sort walks the array $n$ times and each time pulls out the minimum remaining element under our key. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(n)$ extra space — the direct transcription of the phrase "sort by $(\text{rank}, \text{value})$", with the same key the next two rungs use. It shows that the key itself, not the sorting algorithm, is the interesting idea here.

**Selection sort, in plain words.** Every pass scans the not-yet-emitted part of the array, finds the minimum element under the chosen key, and appends it to the output. Cost is $O(n)$ per pass $\times$ $n$ passes $= O(n^2)$. No clever data structure — just repeated "who's the smallest left?".

**Worked example.** `arr1 = [2, 3, 1, 4, 7]`, `arr2 = [2, 1, 4, 3]` gives rank map $\{2{:}0, 1{:}1, 4{:}2, 3{:}3\}$ and sentinel $= 4$. Pass 1: keys $[(0,2),(3,3),(1,1),(2,4),(4,7)]$ — minimum is $(0,2)$, emit $2$. Pass 2: minimum of remaining is $(1,1)$, emit $1$. Pass 3: $(2,4)$, emit $4$. Pass 4: $(3,3)$, emit $3$. Pass 5: $(4,7)$, emit $7$. Result $[2, 1, 4, 3, 7]$ — which is exactly what the built-in key sort produces.

### Problem: Maximum Gap {#sec-srt-p3-b}

::: {.p-statement}
An integer array `nums` ($1 \le n \le 10^5$, $0 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 10^9$). Return the **maximum difference between two successive elements in the sorted array**; return $0$ if $n < 2$. LC requires a **linear-time**, linear-extra-space algorithm — a plain sort is $O(n\log n)$ and only a stepping stone.

Source: [LC 164 · Maximum Gap](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-gap/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example: `nums = [3,6,9,1]` → sorted $[1,3,6,9]$, successive gaps $2,3,3$ → answer $3$. `nums = [10]` → $0$.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The answer is a gap between neighbours *in sorted order*, so the naive route sorts. But the values span $10^9$ — far too wide to count (@sec-srt-p3-a's histogram is out). Bucket sort's insight rescues it. The $n-1$ successive gaps add up to $\max - \min$, so (an averaging, or pigeonhole, argument) the largest of them is *at least* $\lceil (\max-\min)/(n-1) \rceil$. Cut $[\min, \max]$ into buckets of width $w = \max(1, \lfloor (\max-\min)/(n-1) \rfloor)$, which is at most that bound. Two values in the same bucket differ by at most $w - 1$, so no within-bucket pair can be the answer, and the true gap always lies **between** two buckets. That means each bucket only needs its min and max (2 numbers), and one scan of the non-empty buckets' seams gives the answer in $O(n)$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Test every pair for ``successive in sorted order``.** For each ordered pair $(x, y)$ with $x < y$, check whether any other value $z$ satisfies $x < z < y$; if none does, $(x, y)$ is a successive pair of the sorted array and their difference $y - x$ is a candidate gap. Take the maximum. $O(n^3)$ time with the naive inner check — the direct transcription of the definition.
2. **Sort, then scan neighbours.** `b = sorted(nums)`; answer $= \max (b[i+1] - b[i])$. $O(n\log n)$ — the reference oracle LC disallows as the final word but that proves the bucket answer.
3. **Bucket / pigeonhole, linear.** Put each value in bucket $\lfloor (\mathit{nums}[i]-\min)/\text{width} \rfloor$ keeping only per-bucket min and max. The maximum gap is the largest difference between a non-empty bucket's min and the previous non-empty bucket's max. $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.

**Invariant.** With $\text{width} = \max(1, \lfloor (\max-\min)/(n-1) \rfloor)$ and $\lfloor (\max-\min)/\text{width} \rfloor + 1$ buckets, the answer is $\ge \text{width}$ while any within-bucket difference is $\le \text{width} - 1$; so the maximum successive difference joins the max of one non-empty bucket to the min of the next non-empty bucket, and the seam scan sees every such pair.
:::

::: {.form-next}
The linear algorithm LC demands. Scatter values into equal-width buckets by their position in $[\min, \max]$, keep just each bucket's min and max, and the answer is a seam between non-empty buckets — never inside one. $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.

**The averaging argument, in plain words.** Walk the sorted values from $\min$ to $\max$: you take $n-1$ steps that together cover $\max - \min$, so at least one step is as long as the average, $(\max - \min)/(n-1)$, rounded up. That is why each bucket needs only its two extremes. def gap_bucket(nums):
``` {.python .cell-code}
    n = len(nums)

    mn, mx = min(nums), max(nums)

        return 0
    width = max(1, (mx - mn) // (n - 1))

    bmax = [-math.inf] * nb
```

- All equal ($\min = \max$): return $0$; otherwise `width` and `nb` degenerate.
- Two elements: width $= \max - \min$, the seam is that difference — correct.
- Never compute a within-bucket max gap and think it counts: the averaging bound says the answer is always at a seam, so per bucket you only store min and max.

## Pattern 4: Ranks and sorting by derived keys {#sec-srt-p4}

**From how you sort to what you sort on.** Pattern 3 changed the sorting machinery and kept sorting the values. Pattern 4 keeps the machinery (a plain library sort) and changes the *thing being sorted*: a number computed from the whole array first. Two flavours: **coordinate compression** replaces each value by its rank in `sorted(set(...))` (Rank Transform *is* that dictionary), and **derived-key sorting** sorts counts or any attribute read from a table (Equalize the Array sorts the list of frequencies and forgets the values entirely).

**Recognise it.** "Replace each value by its rank / order-statistic", "values up to $10^9$ but only relative order matters" → compress. Or "sort by how *often* each value appears", "ties broken by value", "order by an attribute you first had to count" → sort on a derived key. The tell is that the sort key is **not** the element itself but a number computed from the whole array first.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Compute the key from the data, then sort/lookup by it.

```text
compression  rank = {v: i+1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(a)))};  [rank[v] for v in a]
derived key  score = Counter(a)  /  any table keyed by value
             sorted(set(a), key=lambda v: (score[v], -v))   # tuple key: primary + tie-break
```

**Invariant.** Compression is order-reflecting and equality-preserving: $\mathit{rank}[a] < \mathit{rank}[b] \iff a < b$, and $\mathit{rank}[a] = \mathit{rank}[b] \iff a = b$. A derived-key sort is stable, so a secondary criterion can be layered by a second sort or folded into the tuple key.
:::

**Complexity.** Compression $O(n\log n)$ time (the sort), $O(n)$ space (set + dict), $O(1)$ lookup per element. Derived-key sort $O(n\log n)$ with an $O(n)$ counting pass first. Both beat any per-element $O(n)$ rescan of the distinct set. If you want to skip the dict and still escape the $O(n \cdot |\text{distinct}|)$ brute rescan, sort the distinct list once and binary-search per element (`bisect_left` + 1): $O(\log n)$ lookup, $O(n\log n)$ overall — the intermediate rung @sec-srt-p4-a walks before settling on the one-line dict.

### Problem: Rank Transform of an Array {#sec-srt-p4-a}

::: {.p-statement}
An array `arr` ($0 \le n \le 10^5$, $-10^9 \le \mathit{arr}[i] \le 10^9$). Replace each element with its **rank**: ranks start at $1$, larger values get larger ranks, equal values share a rank, and ranks are as small as possible. Return the transformed array.

Source: [LC 1331 · Rank Transform of an Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/rank-transform-of-an-array/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}

Example: `arr = [40,10,20,30]` → `[4,1,2,3]`; `arr = [100,100,100]` → `[1,1,1]`; `arr = [37,12,28,9,100,56,80,5,12]` → `[5,3,4,2,8,6,7,1,3]`.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A rank is "how many *distinct* values are strictly smaller, plus one." The moment you see that, the problem is **coordinate compression**: replace a huge, sparse value (up to $10^9$) by its dense index in the sorted list of distinct values — exactly what @sec-srt-a4 promises in one line. Build `sorted(set(arr))`; the position of each value there (1-based) is its rank. Look it up per element and you are done in $O(n\log n)$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Count the smaller ones, per element.** For each value, rank $= 1 + |\{u \in \text{distinct values} : u < v\}|$. $O(n^2)$ time — a direct reading of the definition, and the oracle.
2. **Sort the distinct values once, `bisect_left` per element.** Same definition, but sorted *once* up front so each rank query is a $O(\log n)$ binary search on the sorted distinct list instead of a fresh $O(n)$ scan. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.
3. **Coordinate compression via `sorted(set)` + a dict.** Sort the distinct values once; make a dictionary mapping value $\to$ its 1-based position; map every element through it. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space, but the per-element cost drops from $\log n$ to $O(1)$ and the whole thing fits in two lines.

**Invariant.** After `rank = {v: i+1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(arr)))}`, `rank[v]` equals $1 +$ (number of distinct values below $v$) for every present $v$, because the sorted distinct list places exactly that many values before it — which is precisely the required rank.
:::

When `v` is *present* in `uniq`, that index equals the number of strictly smaller elements — exactly our rank-minus-one. So rank is `bisect_left(...) + 1`.

**Worked example.** `arr = [40, 10, 20, 30]` gives `uniq = [10, 20, 30, 40]`. `bisect_left(uniq, 40) = 3` → rank 4; `= 0` for 10 → rank 1; `= 1` for 20 → rank 2; `= 2` for 30 → rank 3. Result $[4, 1, 2, 3]$ — the same as the brute count, at $O(\log n)$ per lookup instead of $O(n)$.

### Problem: Equalize the Array {#sec-srt-p4-b}

::: {.p-statement}
An array $a$ of $n$ integers is **beautiful** if there is a number $C$ such that every value present in it occurs exactly $C$ times. Remove the fewest elements so that $a$ becomes beautiful, and print that number. There are $t$ test cases ($1 \le t \le 10^4$); in each, $1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ and $1 \le a_i \le 10^9$, and the sum of $n$ over all test cases is at most $2 \cdot 10^5$.

Source: [CF 1490F · Equalize the Array](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1490/F){.solved rating="1500"}

Example: $[1, 3, 2, 1, 4, 2]$ → $2$; $[100, 100, 4, 100]$ → $1$; $[1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 2, 6, 6]$ → $2$ (keep two copies each of $2$, $3$, $6$).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Only the frequencies matter, never the values: count each value, then forget the values and sort the list of counts. For a target count $C$, every value with fewer than $C$ copies is deleted completely and every other value is trimmed to $C$, so you **keep** $C \times (\text{number of values with count} \ge C)$. After sorting the counts $f_0 \le \dots \le f_{m-1}$, the values with count at least $f_i$ are exactly positions $i \dots m-1$, so trying $C = f_i$ costs $O(1)$ and the answer is $n - \max_i f_i \cdot (m - i)$. Sorting on a derived key (the count) turns "how many are at least $C$" into a position.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every target count.** For each $C = 1 \dots n$, add up the deletions over the frequency table: $f$ if $f < C$, else $f - C$. $O(n \cdot m)$ for $m$ distinct values.
2. **Only the frequencies are candidates.** Between two consecutive distinct frequencies the number of values with count $\ge C$ does not change, so raising $C$ keeps more and the best $C$ is one of the frequencies. Try only those: $O(m^2)$.
3. **Sort the frequencies; read the count from the position.** Sort $f$ ascending; for $C = f_i$ exactly $m - i$ values have count $\ge C$ (ties give a smaller $m - i$ at a later index, which the maximum ignores). $O(n + m\log m)$.

**Invariant.** In sorted order, index $i$ splits the values into those with count $< f_i$ (all of $f_0 \dots f_{i-1}$ that are strictly smaller, which are deleted) and those with count $\ge f_i$ (kept at $f_i$ copies each); the kept total $f_i (m - i)$ is never more than the true kept total for $C = f_i$, and equals it at the first index of each tie group.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

## Pattern 5: The median and exchange arguments {#sec-srt-p5}

**From sorting to placing a point.** Patterns 1 to 4 used the sorted order to *read* something: neighbours, an arrangement, ranks, counts. Pattern 5 uses it to *choose* something, a single target point, with A5's theorem. When the objective is a sum of **distances** to a common point, the answer is a median and the proof is an exchange argument: slide the target and count how many items you come closer to versus move away from. Stick Lengths is the plain median (unit weights); Minimum Cost to Make Array Equal is the **weighted** median (each value carries a price per unit distance).

**Recognise it.** "Make all elements equal, cost $=$ total movement", "choose a point minimising $\sum |x_i - t|$", "gather the sticks", any objective that is a sum of **absolute deviations** — with or without a per-item weight. The absence of squares is the tell: absolute values → median; squared values → mean (a different, easier, calculus-flavoured objective).

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Sort, then stand at the (weighted) median; the exchange argument licenses it.

```text
plain     b = sorted(x); t = b[n//2]; cost = sum(|xi - t|)
weighted  pairs = sorted(zip(val, w)); total = sum(w); cum = 0
          for (v, w): cum += w; if 2*cum >= total: t = v; break   # weighted median
```

**Invariant.** Moving the target one step right changes the objective by (weight strictly on the left) $-$ (weight strictly on the right); it is negative while the right holds a strict majority. The first position where the running weight reaches half the total has no majority on either side, hence is a minimiser.
:::

**Complexity.** $O(n\log n)$ time (the sort dominates; the walk and final sum are $O(n)$), $O(n)$ space; a selection algorithm (quickselect) finds the plain median in expected $O(n)$ without a full sort. The oracle is the $O(n \cdot |\text{distinct}|)$ "try every value as target" scan, since the cost function's slope only changes at a data point. Between them sits a rung that needs no median insight at all: sort, build prefix sums (weighted prefix sums for the priced version), and evaluate the cost at every data point in $O(1)$ — $O(n\log n)$ total, exercised in @sec-srt-p5-a and @sec-srt-p5-b. ### Problem: Stick Lengths {#sec-srt-p5-a}

::: {.p-statement}
$n$ sticks with lengths $p_1, \dots, p_n$ ($1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, $1 \le p_i \le 10^9$). In one move you may lengthen or shorten any stick by $1$, and each unit of change costs $1$. Make **all sticks equal** with minimum total cost, and print that cost.

Source: [CSES 1074 · Stick Lengths](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1074){.solved}

Example: `5 / 2 3 1 5 2` → $5$ (choose target $2$: costs $0+1+1+3+0=5$).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Only the *multiset* of lengths matters, so sort. For a target $t$, the cost is $f(t) = \sum_i |p_i - t|$ — a sum of absolute deviations — and @sec-srt-a5's promise is that **the median minimises it**. Exchange argument: slide $t$ one step to the right. Every stick at or left of $t$ becomes one unit more expensive, every stick right of $t$ one unit cheaper, so $f$ changes by $(\# \text{ at or left of } t) - (\# \text{ right of } t)$. While more than half the sticks sit to the right, moving right strictly helps; once at least half sit at or left of $t$, moving right never helps. The turning point is the middle element of the sorted array, $b_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$, which is an actual stick length (for even $n$ every point between the two middle elements ties).
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every candidate target.** The minimiser of a sum of absolute deviations always sits *at* one of the values (between two consecutive values $f$ is linear with a fixed slope, so the turn happens at a data point). For each $t \in \{p_i\}$ compute $\sum_i |p_i - t|$ and keep the minimum. $O(n^2)$ — the oracle.
2. **Sort + prefix sums, evaluate cost at every data point in $O(1)$.** Sort $p$ into $b$; build the running sum $\mathit{pref}[k] = b_0 + \dots + b_{k-1}$. Then for target $t = b[i]$, the cost splits into left-side and right-side closed forms and evaluates in $O(1)$: $\mathit{cost}(b[i]) = b[i](i{+}1) - \mathit{pref}[i{+}1] + (\mathit{pref}[n] - \mathit{pref}[i{+}1]) - b[i](n - i - 1)$. Try every $i$, keep the min. $O(n\log n)$ total (sort dominates).
3. **Sort, take the median.** Answer $= \sum_i |b_i - b_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}|$ where $b$ is the sorted array. $O(n\log n)$ time from the sort; the scan afterwards is $O(n)$.

**Invariant.** With $t = b_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$, at least half the sticks are $\le t$ and at least half are $\ge t$. So stepping right changes $f$ by $(\#\le t) - (\#> t) \ge 0$ and stepping left by $(\#\ge t) - (\#< t) \ge 0$; $f$ is convex (a sum of V-shaped terms), so a point where no single step helps is a global minimum.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.form-next}
The brute force is $O(n^2)$ because each candidate target costs a full $O(n)$ rescan. - $t = b[4] = 5$: $\mathit{lc} = 5 \cdot 5 - 13 = 12$; $\mathit{rc} = 0$; cost $12$.

#### Sort, then gather at the median

::: {.form-next}
The exchange argument in one line: sort, pick the middle element as target, and sum the distances. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ or $O(1)$ extra space. This is @sec-srt-a5's theorem used verbatim — the median minimises absolute deviations. Compared to form 2, we drop the prefix table entirely and evaluate $f$ once, at $b[n/2]$.

**Why the median, in plain words.** Picture the sticks on a number line and stand at position $t$; the cost is your total distance to all of them. Step one unit toward the majority side and you come closer to more sticks than you move away from, so the cost drops. The moment strictly more than half the sticks are behind you, every further step costs net. You stop exactly when neither side has a majority — at the median.

### Problem: Minimum Cost to Make Array Equal {#sec-srt-p5-b}

::: {.p-statement}
Two arrays `nums` and `cost` of the same length $n$ ($1 \le n \le 10^5$), with $\mathit{nums}[i], \mathit{cost}[i] \ge 1$ and at most $10^6$ each. Changing `nums[i]` by $1$ costs $\mathit{cost}[i]$ per unit. Make all elements **equal** with minimum total cost; the answer fits in $2^{53}-1$.

Source: [LC 2448 · Minimum Cost to Make Array Equal](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-cost-to-make-array-equal/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}

Example: `nums = [1,3,5,2], cost = [2,3,1,14]` → $8$ (gather at $2$: $2\cdot1 + 3\cdot1 + 1\cdot3 + 14\cdot0 = 8$). `nums = [2,2,2,2,2], cost = [4,2,8,1,3]` → $0$.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Same objective as @sec-srt-p5-a with one twist: each stick now has a *price tag*. Gathering to $t$ costs $f(t) = \sum_i \mathit{cost}_i \cdot |\mathit{nums}_i - t|$. The exchange argument survives verbatim if you imagine each pair $(\mathit{nums}_i, \mathit{cost}_i)$ as $\mathit{cost}_i$ **clones of a unit-cost stick sitting at** $\mathit{nums}_i$: moving the target one step right changes $f$ by (weight at-or-left) $-$ (weight strictly right). The turn happens where the weight stops being a majority on either side — the **weighted median**: sorting by `nums` and walking cumulative `cost`, the first position where the running weight reaches $\lceil \mathit{total}/2 \rceil$. That crossing point is always one of the `nums` values, so the walk never has to interpolate.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every candidate target.** The same slope argument says an optimal target is one of the `nums` values; for each distinct $t$ compute $\sum_i \mathit{cost}_i |\mathit{nums}_i - t|$ and keep the minimum. $O(n \cdot |\text{distinct}|)$ — the oracle.
2. **Sort + weighted prefix sums, evaluate cost at every value in $O(1)$.** Sort pairs by `nums`; build two tables — $\mathit{pref}_w$ (running weight) and $\mathit{pref}_{ws}$ (running $\mathit{nums} \cdot \mathit{cost}$). For target $v = \mathit{pairs}[i].\mathit{nums}$ the cost is $v \cdot \mathit{pref}_w[i{+}1] - \mathit{pref}_{ws}[i{+}1]$ on the left plus $(\mathit{pref}_{ws}[n] - \mathit{pref}_{ws}[i{+}1]) - v \cdot (\mathit{pref}_w[n] - \mathit{pref}_w[i{+}1])$ on the right. Take the min. $O(n\log n)$ total.
3. **Sort by nums, stop at the weighted median.** Sort the pairs by value; walk them accumulating `cost`. The first value where $2 \cdot \mathit{cum} \ge \mathit{total}$ is the target; answer $= \sum_i \mathit{cost}_i |\mathit{nums}_i - t|$. $O(n\log n)$ time.

**Invariant.** Scanning pairs sorted by $\mathit{nums}$ with `cum` $= \sum_{j \le i} \mathit{cost}_j$: before $2 \cdot \mathit{cum} \ge \mathit{total}$ strictly more weight sits to the right of the current value, so $f$ still decreases when the target moves right; after passing it, at least half the weight sits at-or-left and $f$ never decreases again. The crossing value is therefore a minimiser.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

Same asymptotics as the median form, but a longer code and an extra table.

**Weighted prefix sums, in plain words.** Sort pairs $(v, c)$ by $v$. $\mathit{pref}_w[i{+}1] = c_0 + \dots + c_i$ is the total weight up to (and including) index $i$, and $\mathit{pref}_{ws}[i{+}1] = v_0 c_0 + \dots + v_i c_i$ is the running weighted sum. For target $t = v_i$: the left side $\sum_{j \le i} c_j (v_i - v_j)$ is $v_i \cdot \mathit{pref}_w[i{+}1] - \mathit{pref}_{ws}[i{+}1]$; the right side $\sum_{j > i} c_j (v_j - v_i)$ is $(\mathit{pref}_{ws}[n] - \mathit{pref}_{ws}[i{+}1]) - v_i \cdot (\mathit{pref}_w[n] - \mathit{pref}_w[i{+}1])$. Add them for the total cost.

**Worked example.** Pairs sorted by value: $(1,2), (2,14), (3,3), (5,1)$. $\mathit{pref}_w = [0, 2, 16, 19, 20]$; $\mathit{pref}_{ws} = [0, 2, 30, 39, 44]$. At $v = 1$: $\mathit{lc} = 1 \cdot 2 - 2 = 0$, $\mathit{rc} = (44-2) - 1 \cdot 18 = 24$, cost $24$. At $v = 2$: $\mathit{lc} = 2 \cdot 16 - 30 = 2$, $\mathit{rc} = (44-30) - 2 \cdot 4 = 6$, cost $8$. At $v = 3$: $\mathit{lc} = 3 \cdot 19 - 39 = 18$, $\mathit{rc} = (44-39) - 3 \cdot 1 = 2$, cost $20$. At $v = 5$: $\mathit{lc} = 5 \cdot 20 - 44 = 56$, $\mathit{rc} = 0$, cost $56$. Minimum $= 8$, at $v = 2$ — matching LC's answer.

#### Sort by nums, stop at the weighted median

::: {.form-next}
The Hard-problem prize in five lines: sort the pairs by value, accumulate weights, stop where the running weight reaches half the total, then sum deviations to that target. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.

**Weighted median, in plain words.** A weight is how loud a value shouts in the cost. Lined up by value, the cost-minimising target is where the crowd on either side can no longer outvote the other: the first value whose cumulative weight (from the left) is at least half of all weight. With every weight equal to $1$ this is exactly the ordinary median of @sec-srt-p5-a — nothing new is proved, only counted with prices attached.

**Worked example.** Pairs sorted by `nums`: $(1,2), (2,14), (3,3), (5,1)$; total weight $20$. Running cum: $2, 16, 19, 20$. The first with $2 \cdot \mathit{cum} \ge 20$ is the value $2$ (cum $16$). Cost $= 2\cdot1 + 14\cdot0 + 3\cdot1 + 1\cdot3 = 8$ — matches the oracle.

::: {.p-complexity}
**Try every target** is $O(n \cdot |\text{distinct}|)$ time. **Sort + weighted prefix** is $O(n\log n)$ time (sort dominates; two tables and an $O(n)$ scan) and $O(n)$ space for the pairs plus two prefix vectors. **Weighted median** is $O(n\log n)$ time (sort dominates; the walk and final sum are $O(n)$) and $O(n)$ space, and collapses the whole computation to a single target evaluation once the majority-weight position is found. Compare with a *prefix-sum over values* solution, $O(V + n)$ with $V = 10^6$ — a counting-sort flavour (@sec-srt-p3-a) that trades $\log n$ for the value range; the median route is shorter to write and never cares how wide $V$ is.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All `nums` equal: every deviation is $0$, answer $0$ — the walk still lands on that value.
- Weights up to $10^6$ each and $n$ up to $10^5$: `total` reaches $10^{11}$ and the answer may reach the promised bound $2^{53}-1$ — 64-bit is mandatory.

**Looking back.** Five ways a sort earns its $O(n\log n)$, each one idea past the last. Neighbours (P1) make the answer *local*. Comparators (P2) make an order you designed *legitimate*, whether it is a tuple key or an exchange rule. Counting and buckets (P3) trade the value range for linearity. Ranks and derived keys (P4) sort something computed from the array (ranks, counts) instead of the elements. The median and its weighted version (P5) turn a cost function into a position. The thread through all ten problems is the same: pay for the sort once, and the question that remains is a single linear pass over the sorted order. None of them is "a sorting algorithm"; the Sorting Algorithms and Linear-Time Sorting chapters own that, and the next chapter, @sec-bst, spends the remaining purchase, monotonicity, on binary search.

## Pattern map

| Signal in the statement | Pattern | Section |
|---|---|---|
| "Closest pair", "minimum absolute difference", two-team seam | Sort, then scan neighbours | @sec-srt-p1 |
| "Rebuild an order", sort by several fields with mixed directions | Tuple key (prove the greedy after it) | @sec-srt-p2-a |
| "Arrange pieces to maximise/minimise", order depends on two items together | Exchange argument → comparator → key | @sec-srt-p2-b |
| Values in a small fixed range with an order to respect | Counting sort (histogram + emit) | @sec-srt-p3-a |
| "Maximum successive gap" over a $10^9$ range, linear time required | Buckets + averaging bound | @sec-srt-p3-b |
| "Replace by rank", values up to $10^9$ but only order matters | Coordinate compression `sorted(set)` | @sec-srt-p4-a |
| "Every value occurs the same number of times", only counts matter | Sort the frequencies, read counts from positions | @sec-srt-p4-b |
| "Make all equal, cost $=$ total movement" | Median | @sec-srt-p5-a |
